title: Mara, you are seen
hook: Mara comes as an ox, a farmer, a voice of doubt; each time he is recognized (SN 4)
tomorrow: What does being a woman matter

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king's frown at a daughter's birth, and your line, a daughter may be better. Today a whole chapter of disguises, and one sentence that ends every one.

The monks have set their alms bowls out in the open to dry. An ox wanders toward them, big and clumsy. One monk says to another, that ox is going to break the bowls. Another day, a farmer walks past with a plow on his shoulder and a goad in his hand, asking if anyone's seen his oxen. Another day, there's just a voice, whispering that you're wasting your life. Same visitor, every time, in a different coat. The Samyutta gives him a whole chapter.
screen: `AN OX NEAR THE DRYING BOWLS.` → `A FARMER WITH A PLOW.` → `THE SAME VISITOR, NEW COAT.`

segments.voice: Mara is the tempter in the Buddhist texts, the one who wants beings to stay caught. His name is linked to death, and he's sometimes called the Evil One. The fourth chapter of the Connected Sayings is all Mara, a run of short scenes with a pattern. Mara shows up, often in disguise: a huge elephant king in the dark, a serpent, the ox by the bowls, a farmer who argues that the eye and the ear and all the senses belong to him. Sometimes he's just a voice: you're not really awake, why bother, go back to ordinary pleasures. And every time, the Buddha recognizes him. That's the turn. He doesn't fight, flee, or argue for an hour. He knows: this is Mara, and often says so in a short verse. Then comes the line that closes scene after scene, almost a refrain: Mara, realizing the Blessed One knows me, sad and disappointed, disappears right there. Being seen is enough. Read as psychology, the chapter is strikingly practical. Temptation rarely announces itself. It arrives as something ordinary, a heavy animal, a reasonable farmer, a sensible voice of doubt. The power lies in the disguise; once it's named, much of that power is gone. Buddhist schools differ on how literally to take Mara. Some traditional readers take him as a real being, a deity of the desire realm. Some modern teachers read him as a picture of craving and fear. The texts can hold both.
screen: `MARA: THE ONE WHO KEEPS BEINGS CAUGHT` · `AN ELEPHANT, A SERPENT, AN OX, A FARMER` · `EVERY TIME, HE IS RECOGNIZED` · `THE BLESSED ONE KNOWS ME, AND HE GOES` · then, large: `I SEE YOU, MARA.`

segments.voice: Think of one temptation that keeps visiting you, the extra scroll, the sharp reply, the voice that says skip it, and picture the disguise it usually wears: tired, reasonable, deserved. Quietly, or aloud if you're alone, name it in a plain sentence, not angry, not afraid, the way you'd greet an old acquaintance at the door: I see you. Then let the breath carry on, and notice what happens to the pull once it's been named.
Mara. The tempter of the Buddhist texts, whose name means death; in SN 4 he comes in disguise again and again, and each time he is recognized and disappears. Today's word.
Your line: I see you, Mara. The power was in the disguise all along. That's day six hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Buddhist art across Asia shows Mara and his armies at the night of the awakening, and some meditation teachers encourage students to name distractions and cravings as they arise, sometimes playfully as visits from Mara.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit Mara: the tempter, from a root meaning death, to die or to kill.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mara is a Buddhist devil.
what it means: the tempter of the texts, who keeps beings caught; in SN 4 he loses his power the moment he is recognized.

what a scholar hears: the Mara Samyutta gathers its episodes in one place; the refrain where he realizes he has been seen and vanishes closes many of them, and later traditions speak of several Maras, including the defilements and death itself.

chat.says: In the old Buddhist stories, how does the Buddha deal with Mara?
options: He recognizes him. Once Mara knows he's been seen, he disappears.
He argues with him for hours, until Mara finally runs out of points.
He hides in deep meditation until Mara gets bored and leaves.
chat.meaning: In SN 4, scene after scene ends the same way: the Buddha knows Mara, and Mara, seen, disappears. The power was in the disguise.

Mara.meaning: the tempter of the Buddhist texts, linked to death

Samyutta.meaning: the Connected Sayings, a big collection of short discourses
